source_refs.note: Book p. 182-184: 10.2 definition, identity sets, Note, rules 1-3, table and sign chart, (a)/(b), Examples 3-4. Book errors: cos(pi/2+t), sin(3pi/2-t) signs; Ex 3(iii) 4x90 and +1, (iv) +2/sqrt3; Ex 4 tan(270+t)=cot t, answer tan t.

blocks.text: Two angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are said to be allied if \(\alpha \pm \beta = n(90^{\circ})\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
For example, \(\pm\alpha\), \(90^{\circ} \pm \alpha\), \(180^{\circ} \pm \alpha\), \(270^{\circ} \pm \alpha\) and \(360^{\circ} \pm \alpha\) are some allied angles of \(\alpha\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In simple words: two angles are allied when their sum or their difference is a whole number of right angles. For example \(30^{\circ}\) and \(60^{\circ}\) (sum \(90^{\circ}\)), \(30^{\circ}\) and \(150^{\circ}\) (sum \(180^{\circ}\)), \(30^{\circ}\) and \(210^{\circ}\) (difference \(180^{\circ}\)). Their trigonometric ratios are closely related, so the ratios of a large angle can be found from those of an acute angle.
Using the fundamental law of trigonometry, \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\), and its deductions, we derive the following identities:

\[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cos\theta\]
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \sin\theta\]
\[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cot\theta\]
\[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \cos\theta\]
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \sin\theta\]
\[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = -\cot\theta\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \sin\theta\). The correct identity is \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = -\sin\theta\), as proved in 10.1.2, result (ii): \(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\) is in quadrant II, where cos is negative.

\[\sin(\pi-\theta) = \sin\theta\]
\[\cos(\pi-\theta) = -\cos\theta\]
\[\tan(\pi-\theta) = -\tan\theta\]
\[\sin(\pi+\theta) = -\sin\theta\]
\[\cos(\pi+\theta) = -\cos\theta\]
\[\tan(\pi+\theta) = \tan\theta\]

\[\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cos\theta\]
\[\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = -\sin\theta\]
\[\tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cot\theta\]
\[\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = -\cos\theta\]
\[\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \sin\theta\]
\[\tan\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = -\cot\theta\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cos\theta\). The correct identity is \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = -\cos\theta\): \(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\) is in quadrant III, where sin is negative. The book itself gives \(-\cos\theta\) in part (a)(iii) below.

\[\sin(2\pi-\theta) = -\sin\theta\]
\[\cos(2\pi-\theta) = \cos\theta\]
\[\tan(2\pi-\theta) = -\tan\theta\]
\[\sin(2\pi+\theta) = \sin\theta\]
\[\cos(2\pi+\theta) = \cos\theta\]
\[\tan(2\pi+\theta) = \tan\theta\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Each line can be proved from 10.1.2. For example \(\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\pi\cos\theta - \cos\pi\sin\theta = 0 - (-1)\sin\theta = \sin\theta\), using \(\sin\pi = 0\), \(\cos\pi = -1\). You do not need to memorise all 24 lines: the device below gives any of them in a few seconds.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The above results also apply to the reciprocals of sine, cosine and tangent. These results are used frequently in the study of trigonometry, and they can be remembered by the following device:

items: If \(\theta\) is added to or subtracted from an odd multiple of a right angle, the trigonometric ratios change into co-ratios and vice versa, i.e. sin \(\rightleftarrows\) cos, tan \(\rightleftarrows\) cot, sec \(\rightleftarrows\) cosec. E.g. \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cos\theta\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \sin\theta\).
If \(\theta\) is added to or subtracted from an even multiple of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), the trigonometric ratios remain the same.

The sign of the result is decided by the quadrant in which the terminal arm of the angle lies. E.g. \(\sin(\pi-\theta) = \sin\theta\), \(\tan(\pi+\theta) = \tan\theta\), \(\cos(2\pi-\theta) = \cos\theta\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How to use the device, for example \(\cos(\pi + \theta)\): \(\pi = 2 \times \frac{\pi}{2}\) is an even multiple, so cos stays cos. Take \(\theta\) as if it were acute: \(\pi + \theta\) then lies in quadrant III, where cos is negative. So \(\cos(\pi + \theta) = -\cos\theta\). Treating θ as acute is only a way to decide the sign; the identities are true for every θ.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Remember the chart anticlockwise from quadrant I as A, S, T, C (“All Students Take Coffee”): All ratios positive in I, Sin (and cosec) in II, Tan (and cot) in III, Cos (and sec) in IV. Every other ratio is negative in that quadrant.

(a) In \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\), \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)\), \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\) and \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right)\), odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) are involved. Therefore, sin will change into cos. Moreover, the angle of measure

items: (i) \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\) will have terminal side in Quad. I, so \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = \cos\theta\);
(ii) \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)\) will have terminal side in Quad. II, so \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = \cos\theta\);
(iii) \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\) will have terminal side in Quad. III, so \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right) = -\cos\theta\);
(iv) \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right)\) will have terminal side in Quad. IV, so \(\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\theta\right) = -\cos\theta\).

blocks.text: (b) In \(\cos(\pi-\theta)\), \(\cos(\pi+\theta)\), \(\cos(2\pi-\theta)\) and \(\cos(2\pi+\theta)\), even multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) are involved. Therefore, cos will remain as cos. Moreover, the angle of measure

items: (i) \((\pi-\theta)\) will have terminal side in Quad. II, therefore \(\cos(\pi-\theta) = -\cos\theta\);
(ii) \((\pi+\theta)\) will have terminal side in Quad. III, so \(\cos(\pi+\theta) = -\cos\theta\);
(iii) \((2\pi-\theta)\) will have terminal side in Quad. IV, so \(\cos(2\pi-\theta) = \cos\theta\);
(iv) \((2\pi+\theta)\) will have terminal side in Quad. I, so \(\cos(2\pi+\theta) = \cos\theta\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For a negative angle, first take the minus sign out: \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\), \(\cot(-\theta) = -\cot\theta\), \(\operatorname{cosec}(-\theta) = -\operatorname{cosec}\theta\), but \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\sec(-\theta) = \sec\theta\). Then apply the device to the positive angle. Example 3 (iii) and (iv) use this.

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem:
Without using the tables, write down the values of:
(i) \(\sin 225^{\circ}\)  (ii) \(\tan 600^{\circ}\)  (iii) \(\cot(-225^{\circ})\)  (iv) \(\operatorname{cosec}(-420^{\circ})\)
steps:
Given: the angles \(225^{\circ}\), \(600^{\circ}\), \(-225^{\circ}\) and \(-420^{\circ}\).
To find: the exact value of each ratio without tables.
Method: write each angle as \(n \times 90^{\circ} \pm \theta\) with \(\theta\) acute. If \(n\) is even the ratio stays the same; if \(n\) is odd it changes to its co-ratio. The sign is that of the ORIGINAL ratio in the quadrant of the whole angle. A negative angle is first made positive.

(i) Find sin 225°
\[\sin 225^{\circ} = \sin(180^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= \sin(2 \times 90^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= -\sin 45^{\circ} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(n = 2\) is even, so sin stays sin. \(225^{\circ}\) lies in quadrant III (between \(180^{\circ}\) and \(270^{\circ}\)), where sin is negative.

(ii) Find tan 600°
\[\tan 600^{\circ} = \tan(540^{\circ} + 60^{\circ})\]
\[= \tan(6 \times 90^{\circ} + 60^{\circ})\]
\[= \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}\]
Why: \(n = 6\) is even, so tan stays tan. \(600^{\circ} = 360^{\circ} + 240^{\circ}\) ends in quadrant III, where tan is positive.

(iii) Find cot(−225°)
\[\cot(-225^{\circ}) = -\cot 225^{\circ}\]
\[= -\cot(180^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= -\cot(2 \times 90^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= -\cot 45^{\circ} = -1\]
Why: \(\cot(-\theta) = -\cot\theta\). Then \(180^{\circ} = 2 \times 90^{\circ}\) is an even multiple, so cot stays cot, and \(225^{\circ}\) is in quadrant III where cot is positive: \(\cot 225^{\circ} = +\cot 45^{\circ} = 1\). With the minus sign in front the value is \(-1\).
The book prints this line as \(-\cot(180 + 45)^{\circ} = \) \(-\cot(4\times 90+45)^{\circ} = -(-\cot 45^{\circ}) = 1\) (see the Book correction below).

(iv) Find cosec(−420°)
\[\operatorname{cosec}(-420^{\circ}) = -\operatorname{cosec} 420^{\circ}\]
\[= -\operatorname{cosec}(360^{\circ} + 60^{\circ})\]
\[= -\operatorname{cosec}(4 \times 90^{\circ} + 60^{\circ})\]
\[= -\operatorname{cosec} 60^{\circ} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\]
Why: \(\operatorname{cosec}(-\theta) = -\operatorname{cosec}\theta\). \(n = 4\) is even, so cosec stays cosec; \(420^{\circ} = 360^{\circ} + 60^{\circ}\) ends in quadrant I where cosec is positive, so \(\operatorname{cosec} 420^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\). The minus sign in front stays.
The book ends this line with \(-\operatorname{cosec} 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), dropping the minus sign.

Check: reduce each angle by a full period instead
(i) \(\sin 225^{\circ} \approx -0.7071 = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
(ii) tan repeats every \(180^{\circ}\): \(\tan 600^{\circ} = \tan(600^{\circ} - 540^{\circ}) = \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}\).
(iii) cot repeats every \(180^{\circ}\): \(\cot(-225^{\circ}) = \cot(-45^{\circ}) = -1\).
(iv) cosec repeats every \(360^{\circ}\): \(\operatorname{cosec}(-420^{\circ}) = \operatorname{cosec}(-60^{\circ}) = -\frac{1}{\sin 60^{\circ}} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
(iii) The book prints \(-\cot(180 + 45)^{\circ} = -\cot(4\times 90+45)^{\circ} = -(-\cot 45^{\circ}) = 1\). Here \(180^{\circ} = 2 \times 90^{\circ}\) (not \(4 \times 90^{\circ}\)), and \(\cot 225^{\circ} = +\cot 45^{\circ}\) because cot is positive in quadrant III. So \(\cot(-225^{\circ}) = -\cot 45^{\circ} = -1\), not 1.
(iv) The book prints \(-\operatorname{cosec} 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\). Correct: \(-\operatorname{cosec} 60^{\circ} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(\operatorname{cosec}(-420^{\circ}) = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).

blocks.title: Example 4
steps:
Given: a fraction of six trigonometric ratios of allied angles.
To find: its simplest form in terms of \(\theta\).
Method: reduce each ratio to a ratio of \(\theta\) with the device (odd or even multiple of \(90^{\circ}\), then the sign from the quadrant), substitute, and cancel common factors.

Step 1: Reduce the numerator ratios
\[\sin(180^{\circ}-\theta) = \sin\theta\]
\[\cos(360^{\circ}-\theta) = \cos\theta\]
\[\tan(90^{\circ}+\theta) = -\cot\theta\]
Why: \(180^{\circ}\) and \(360^{\circ}\) are even multiples of \(90^{\circ}\), so sin and cos stay; \(180^{\circ}-\theta\) is in quadrant II (sin positive) and \(360^{\circ}-\theta\) in quadrant IV (cos positive). \(90^{\circ}\) is an odd multiple, so tan becomes cot; \(90^{\circ}+\theta\) is in quadrant II, where tan is negative.

Step 2: Reduce the denominator ratios
\[\sin(90^{\circ}-\theta) = \cos\theta\]
\[\cos(180^{\circ}+\theta) = -\cos\theta\]
\[\tan(270^{\circ}+\theta) = -\cot\theta\]
Why: \(90^{\circ}-\theta\): odd multiple, sin becomes cos, quadrant I, positive. \(180^{\circ}+\theta\): even multiple, cos stays, quadrant III, negative. \(270^{\circ} = 3 \times 90^{\circ}\) is an odd multiple, so tan becomes cot; \(270^{\circ}+\theta\) is in quadrant IV, where tan is negative, so the result is \(-\cot\theta\).
The book prints \(\tan(270^{\circ}+\theta) = \cot\theta\) here, without the minus sign (see the Book correction below).

Step 3: Substitute
\[\dfrac{\sin\theta\cdot\cos\theta\cdot(-\cot\theta)}{\cos\theta\cdot(-\cos\theta)\cdot(-\cot\theta)}\]
Why: each ratio is replaced by its reduced form from Steps 1 and 2.

Step 4: Simplify
\[= \dfrac{-\sin\theta\cos\theta\cot\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta\cot\theta}\]
\[= \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = -\tan\theta\]
Why: in the denominator \((-\cos\theta)(-\cot\theta) = +\cos\theta\cot\theta\). Then \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) cancel from top and bottom, and \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\).
With \(+\cot\theta\) in the denominator, the book ends with \(\frac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\).

Check: put \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\)
\[\text{Num.} = \sin 150^{\circ}\cos 330^{\circ}\tan 120^{\circ}\]
\[= \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot(-\sqrt{3}) = -\tfrac{3}{4}\]
\[\text{Den.} = \sin 60^{\circ}\cos 210^{\circ}\tan 300^{\circ}\]
\[= \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\cdot(-\sqrt{3}) = \tfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}\]
\[\text{Num.} \div \text{Den.} = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = -\tan 30^{\circ}\]
The numerical value agrees with \(-\tan\theta\), not with \(\tan\theta\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\tan(270^{\circ}+\theta) = \cot\theta\). Correct: \(\tan(270^{\circ}+\theta) = -\cot\theta\) (odd multiple, so tan becomes cot; quadrant IV, where tan is negative), as in the book's own table of identities. With this sign the denominator is \(\cos\theta(-\cos\theta)(-\cot\theta) = \cos^{2}\theta\cot\theta\), and the answer is \(-\tan\theta\), not the printed \(\frac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Allied angles: \(\alpha \pm \beta = n(90^{\circ})\), for example \(90^{\circ} \pm \theta\), \(180^{\circ} \pm \theta\), \(270^{\circ} \pm \theta\), \(360^{\circ} \pm \theta\).
2. Odd multiple of \(90^{\circ}\): sin \(\leftrightarrow\) cos, tan \(\leftrightarrow\) cot, sec \(\leftrightarrow\) cosec. Even multiple: the ratio stays.
3. The sign is that of the original ratio in the quadrant of the whole angle (θ taken acute).
4. Quadrant signs: All (I), Sin (II), Tan (III), Cos (IV).
5. For a negative angle, take the minus out first; cos and sec are even, the other four ratios are odd.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the sign from the new ratio. For \(\tan(270^{\circ}+\theta)\) the sign comes from tan in quadrant IV (negative), even though the answer is written with cot: \(-\cot\theta\). This is exactly the slip in the book's Example 4.
2. Counting the multiple wrongly: \(180^{\circ} = 2 \times 90^{\circ}\) (even), \(270^{\circ} = 3 \times 90^{\circ}\) (odd), \(540^{\circ} = 6 \times 90^{\circ}\) (even).
3. Forgetting the minus sign taken out of a negative angle, as in the book's Example 3 (iv).
